usage: 거실 + 이 because the word ends in a consonant; subject of a description
There is a TV in the living room.
static existence uses 에, not 에서
I rest in the living room.
an action happens here, so 에서 replaces 에
거실 as a direct object takes 을
examples: 여기가 거실이에요.
This is the living room.
simplest 이다 sentence introducing a room to a guest
가족이 거실에 모여서 텔레비전을 봐요.
The family gathers in the living room and watches TV.
everyday: 거실 collocates with 모이다 (gather) and 텔레비전을 보다
손님이 오면 거실로 안내해서 소파에 앉으시게 해요.
When guests come, I show them to the living room and seat them on the sofa.
real situation: direction 로 (to the living room) + honorific 앉으시다
nuance: 거실 is the shared 'living/common' room of a Korean home — the social hub where the family relaxes together and where guests are received, almost always centred on a 소파 and a TV. It is Sino-Korean: 居室, literally 居 'to dwell/reside' + 室 'room', so the feel is 'the room you live in (together)'. Contrast it with 응접실 (應接室, a formal parlour for receiving visitors), which sounds old-fashioned and upper-class today, and with 방, the generic word for any closed 'room/bedroom'; 거실 specifically names the open central area. Register is fully neutral — children and adults alike say 거실. The big English-speaker pitfall is location particles: because a TV simply sits there you say 거실에 텔레비전이 있어요 (에 = existence), but because you *do* something there you switch to 거실에서 쉬어요 (에서 = action). Mixing these up (거실에서 텔레비전이 있어요) is the single most common error.

mistakes: Saying 거실에서 소파가 있어요 to mean 'there is a sofa in the living room'. Existence/location of a thing takes 에 (거실에 소파가 있어요); 에서 only marks the place where an action occurs.
Calling the living room 방. 방 means a closed private room (often a bedroom); the open central area is specifically 거실. Use 거실, not 방, for the family room.
Treating 거실 as 'house' and saying 거실에 가요 for 'I'm going home'. To go home you say 집에 가요; 거실 is just one room inside the 집.
usage_note: particle and register notes inline above

usage: 침실 + 이 as subject of a quality
There is a bed in the bedroom.
sleeping is an action, so 에서
examples: 여기는 부모님 침실이에요.
This is my parents' bedroom.
simple 이다 sentence labelling a room
저는 보통 밤 열한 시에 침실에 들어가요.
I usually go into the bedroom at eleven at night.
everyday: 침실에 들어가다 (enter), time with 에
아기가 깰까 봐 침실에서는 발소리를 죽여요.
Afraid the baby might wake, I tread silently in the bedroom.
real situation: topic-marked 에서는 + 발소리를 죽이다 idiom
nuance: 침실 is the private 'sleeping room', Sino-Korean 寢室 from 寢 'to sleep/lie down' + 室 'room' — so literally 'sleep-room', which makes its core meaning easy to remember. It names the room by its function (sleeping), whereas the everyday word 방 is the neutral term for any room and is what Koreans most often say in casual speech ('내 방' = my room) even when they mean their bedroom; 침실 sounds slightly more formal or descriptive, the word you'd see on a floor plan or in a real-estate ad (안방 = the main/master bedroom). Do not confuse it with 거실 (the shared living room) — 침 vs 거 is the whole difference. The English-speaker pitfall is again the 에 / 에서 split: the bed *is there* (침실에 침대가 있어요, existence → 에) but you *sleep* there (침실에서 자요, action → 에서). Also note Koreans rarely say '내 침실'; 내 방 is far more natural for 'my bedroom'.

mistakes: Saying 침실에서 침대가 있어요. The bed's existence takes 에 (침실에 침대가 있어요); reserve 에서 for actions like 자다 or 쉬다.
Insisting on 침실 in casual conversation. To say 'I'm going to my room/bed', Koreans say 내 방에 가요, not 내 침실에 가요 — 방 is the natural everyday word.
Confusing 침실 with 거실. They look alike but 침(寢) = sleep and 거(居) = dwell; 침실 is the bedroom, 거실 is the family living room.
usage_note: function-based naming; 방 is the casual default

usage: 베란다 ends in a vowel, so subject 가
There are flowerpots on the balcony.
I dry laundry on the balcony.
베란다 as object takes 를 after a vowel
examples: 저 집은 베란다가 커요.
That apartment has a big balcony.
simple description with 가
엄마는 베란다에서 고추를 말리고 화분도 키워요.
Mum dries chillies and grows potted plants on the balcony.
everyday: classic 베란다 uses — drying food and 화분 키우다
겨울에는 베란다 문을 닫아서 찬 바람이 안 들어오게 해요.
In winter we shut the balcony door so the cold wind can't get in.
real situation: 닫다 + causative '~게 하다' for keeping cold out
nuance: 베란다 is a loanword (from English 'veranda'), so there is no hanja — and that loan path creates the main pitfall: in Korean apartments 베란다 actually refers to what English calls a *balcony/utility deck*, the enclosed strip off the living room where families keep 화분 (potted plants), dry 빨래 (laundry) and 고추 (chillies), and store overflow. Technically architects distinguish 발코니 (balcony) from 베란다 and from 테라스 (terrace, a ground-level open deck), but in ordinary speech most Koreans just say 베란다 for that apartment space. Contrast it with 마당, the open *yard/ground* of a detached house — 베란다 hangs off an upper-floor flat, 마당 is earth you stand on. Register is fully neutral. Watch the particles: plants simply sit there (베란다에 화분이 있어요, 에) but laundry is actively dried there (베란다에서 빨래를 말려요, 에서); and because it ends in a vowel the subject marker is 가, not 이.

usage: There are shoes at the entrance.
I take off my shoes at the entrance.
taking off is an action → 에서
examples: 여기가 현관이에요.
This is the entryway.
simple labelling sentence
집에 들어올 때는 현관에서 신발을 벗어요.
When entering the house, we take our shoes off at the entrance.
everyday: the core Korean custom, 들어올 때 + 벗다
택배는 그냥 현관 앞에 놓고 가 주세요.
Please just leave the parcel in front of the entrance.
real situation: 현관 앞 (in front of) + polite request 놓고 가 주세요
nuance: 현관 is the indoor 'entry hall' of a home — the small sunken or tiled area just inside the door where you step out of your shoes before going up into the living space. It is Sino-Korean 玄關, literally 玄 'dark/profound' + 關 'barrier/gate', a term originally from Zen architecture meaning the threshold into a dwelling. The all-important cultural point: Koreans always remove shoes at the 현관 (현관에서 신발을 벗어요), so this word carries the whole shoes-off custom. Distinguish it sharply from 대문, the *outer gate* opening from the street into the yard: 대문 is outside on the property line, 현관 is the door/hall of the building itself — an apartment has a 현관 but no 대문. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'entrance' as one undifferentiated word and so reaching for 입구 (the entrance *to* a public place like a station or shop); for the entry of a *home* you must use 현관, and remember existence is 에 (신발이 현관에 있어요) but the act of removing shoes is 에서.

Saying 현관에서 신발이 있어요. The shoes' existence takes 에 (현관에 신발이 있어요); use 에서 only with the action 벗다 (take off).
usage_note: carries the shoes-off custom; not 입구

usage: 지붕 + 이; note ㅎ-irregular 빨갛다 → 빨개요
Snow piles up on the roof.
snow accumulating on a surface → 에
A sound comes from the roof.
examples: 저 집은 지붕이 빨개요.
That house has a red roof.
simple description; ㅎ-irregular adjective in 요-form
비가 오면 지붕에서 빗소리가 나요.
When it rains, you hear the sound of rain on the roof.
everyday: 비가 오다 condition + 소리가 나다 collocation
태풍에 지붕이 날아가서 동네가 난리가 났어요.
The typhoon blew the roof off and the neighbourhood was in chaos.
real situation: 날아가다 (be blown away) + 난리가 나다 idiom
nuance: 지붕 is the *outside* top cover of a building — the slates, tiles or concrete that shed rain, snow and sun. It is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja). The sharp, must-learn contrast is 지붕 vs 천장: 지붕 is the roof you see from *outside* and birds land on, while 천장 (天障, 'sky-barrier') is the *inside* upper surface of a room with the light fixed to it. English uses 'roof' loosely for both ('the roof of the room'), which is exactly the trap — looking up indoors at the light you must say 천장, never 지붕. 지붕 collocates with weather and damage verbs: 눈이 쌓이다 (snow piles up), 비가 새다 (rain leaks through), 날아가다 (be blown off). Register is neutral and concrete. Also note the colour example uses the ㅎ-irregular adjective 빨갛다, which drops the ㅎ and becomes 빨개요 in the polite form — a small but frequent stumbling block.

Saying 지붕에서 눈이 있어요 for 'there's snow on the roof'. Snow's presence takes 에 (지붕에 눈이 있어요); 에서 marks where an action/sound happens.
Conjugating the colour as 빨갛아요. 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular: drop ㅎ and add 요 → 빨개요 (지붕이 빨개요).
usage_note: outside cover; pairs with weather verbs

usage: There is a painting on the wall.
I hang a clock on the wall.
attaching to the wall surface uses 에, not 에서
examples: 이 벽은 좀 얇아요.
This wall is a bit thin.
simple description with topic 은
저는 벽에 가족사진을 붙여 놨어요.
I've put family photos up on the wall.
everyday: 붙이다 + resultative '~아 놓다' (have it stuck up)
옆집 소리가 벽을 타고 다 들려서 좀 불편해요.
Sound from next door travels through the wall, which is a bit uncomfortable.
real situation: 벽을 타고 (travelling along the wall) + 들리다
nuance: 벽 is a *vertical* dividing surface — the side of a room, the partition between flats, or a freestanding masonry wall — and it is the surface things get hung *on*. It is Sino-Korean 壁. Two contrasts matter. First, 벽 vs 바닥/천장: 벽 is the upright side, 바닥 the floor underfoot, 천장 the surface overhead. Second, 벽 vs 담(장): a 벽 is typically a *building/structural* wall, whereas 담 or 담장 is the *outer boundary wall/fence* around a yard — English 'wall' covers both, so don't say 벽 for the wall enclosing a garden (that's 담). The decisive English-speaker pitfall is the particle for hanging: you hang a picture *on* the wall, but Korean uses 에 (the destination/surface), not 에서 — 벽에 그림을 걸어요, never 벽에서. 벽 collocates with 걸다 (hang), 붙이다 (stick), 기대다 (lean against). Note the colour example again rides the ㅎ-irregular: 하얗다 → 하얘요.

Conjugating 하얗다 as 하얗아요. It is ㅎ-irregular: 벽이 하얘요 (drop ㅎ, contract to 얘).

usage: There is a bag on the floor.
sitting down onto the floor surface → 에
examples: 바닥이 미끄러워요.
The floor is slippery.
simple description; ㅂ-irregular 미끄럽다 → 미끄러워요
우리는 보통 바닥에 앉아서 밥을 먹어요.
We usually sit on the floor to eat.
everyday: the 좌식 (floor-sitting) custom, 앉아서 + 먹다
겨울에는 보일러를 켜면 바닥이 뜨끈뜨끈해져요.
In winter, when you turn on the boiler the floor gets toasty warm.
real situation: 온돌/보일러 heated floor + mimetic 뜨끈뜨끈 + 해지다 (become)
nuance: 바닥 is the *floor* you stand, sit and (with 온돌 under-floor heating) even sleep on — a native-Korean word with no hanja. Its core sense is broader than English 'floor': 바닥 means the *bottom surface* of anything, so it also covers the bed/bottom of a pan, a river or the sea (강 바닥, 바다 바닥), and figuratively 'rock bottom' (가격이 바닥이다 = the price has hit bottom). For the part of a building you must not confuse it with 마루 (a wooden-floored area/hall) or with 층, which means a *storey/level* of a building — '2층' is the second floor *as a level*, but the surface you walk on is 바닥. Because Korean homes are heated through the floor, 바닥 collocates strongly with 따뜻하다/뜨겁다 (warm/hot) and with 앉다 and 닦다. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 층 when you mean the physical surface, and remember sitting *down onto* the floor uses 에 (바닥에 앉아요). The temperature words 차갑다/미끄럽다 are ㅂ-irregular → 차가워요/미끄러워요.

Saying 바닥에서 가방이 있어요. The bag's presence takes 에 (바닥에 가방이 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action.
Conjugating 차갑다 as 차갑아요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 바닥이 차가워요 (ㅂ → 워).

usage: 천장 + 이 as subject of a quality
There is a light on the ceiling.
I look up at the ceiling.
examples: 이 방은 천장이 높아요.
This room has a high ceiling.
simple description; 천장 collocates with 높다/낮다
천장에 달린 등이 너무 어두워요.
The light hanging from the ceiling is too dim.
everyday: 천장에 달리다 (hung from the ceiling) modifying 등
윗집에서 물이 새는지 천장에 얼룩이 생겼어요.
A stain has appeared on the ceiling, maybe the flat above is leaking.
real situation: 물이 새다 (leak) + 얼룩이 생기다 (a stain forms)
nuance: 천장 is the *inside* upper surface of a room — what you see when you lie down and look up, with the 등 (light) fixed to it. It is Sino-Korean 天障, literally 天 'sky' + 障 'barrier/screen', i.e. the 'sky-screen' overhead, a nice image for the indoor counterpart of the sky. The essential contrast is 천장 vs 지붕: 천장 is *inside* (ceiling), 지붕 is *outside* (roof). English collapses both into 'roof/ceiling' loosely, which is the main trap — indoors, always 천장. 천장 pairs with 높다/낮다 (high/low), 등이 달리다 (a light is hung), and 물이 새다/얼룩이 생기다 for leak damage. Register is neutral and descriptive. The particle pitfall is the familiar one: the light *is mounted* there (천장에 등이 있어요, 에) but water *drips* there (천장에서 물이 떨어져요, 에서, because dripping is the action/source). Memory hook: 천(天, sky) is up high → ceiling; 지붕 starts with 지 like 지구(earth)'s outer shell.

structuredNuance.t: 천장 is the inside upper surface of a room — what you see when you lie down and look up, with the 등 (light) fixed to it. 천장 pairs with 높다/낮다 (high/low), 등이 달리다 (a light is hung), and 물이 새다/얼룩이 생기다 for leak damage. Register is neutral and descriptive.
The essential contrast is 천장 vs 지붕: 천장 is inside (ceiling), 지붕 is outside (roof). Memory hook: 천(天, sky) is up high → ceiling; 지붕 starts with 지 like 지구(earth)'s outer shell.
It is Sino-Korean 天障, literally 天 'sky' + 障 'barrier/screen', i.e. the 'sky-screen' overhead, a nice image for the indoor counterpart of the sky.

English collapses both 천장 and 지붕 into 'roof/ceiling' loosely, which is the main trap — indoors, always 천장. The particle pitfall is the familiar one: the light is mounted there (천장에 등이 있어요, 에) but water drips there (천장에서 물이 떨어져요, 에서, because dripping is the action/source).

mistakes: Saying 지붕 for the indoor ceiling. The inside surface with the light is 천장; 지붕 is the outdoor roof only.
Saying 천장에서 등이 있어요. A mounted light's existence takes 에 (천장에 등이 있어요); reserve 에서 for the dripping/leaking action.
Pronouncing/writing it 천정. The standard form is 천장 (天障); 천정 is a common but non-standard variant — use 천장.

usage: 마당 + 이; 넓다 (be wide/spacious) is the natural pairing
There is a tree in the yard.
마당 as object takes 을; 쓸다 (sweep)
examples: 우리 집에는 마당이 있어요.
Our house has a yard.
simple existence sentence; topic 집에는 + 마당이 있다
아이들이 마당에서 강아지랑 뛰어놀아요.
The children run around the yard with the puppy.
everyday: 마당에서 + 뛰어놀다, comitative 랑
여름이면 마당에 평상을 깔고 삼겹살을 구워 먹어요.
Come summer, we set out a wooden bench in the yard and grill pork belly.
real situation: 평상을 깔다 + 구워 먹다, a vivid Korean summer scene
nuance: 마당 is the open *ground/yard* belonging to a detached house — bare earth or paving where the family dries crops, sweeps leaves, sets out a 평상, or grills meat in summer. It is a native-Korean word (no hanja) and carries a warm, traditional, single-house feel; an apartment dweller does *not* have a 마당, so the word itself implies a 단독주택 (detached home). Distinguish it sharply from 정원 (庭園), a cultivated ornamental *garden* with planned flowers and lawn — 마당 is plain working ground, 정원 is decorative; and from 베란다, the small deck off an apartment. Figuratively 마당 can even mean an 'occasion/situation' (이 마당에 = 'at this point/in this situation'), though beginners can set that aside. 마당 collocates with 넓다 (spacious), 쓸다 (sweep), 놀다 (play), 나무/꽃이 있다. Register is neutral and homely. Pitfall: don't use 마당 for an apartment's outdoor space (that's 베란다), and keep 에 for existence (마당에 나무가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions (마당에서 놀아요).

mistakes: Using 마당 for an apartment's outdoor deck. 마당 is the ground of a detached house; an apartment's outdoor strip is 베란다.

usage: 울타리 ends in a vowel → subject 가
flowers on the fence surface → 에
leaning against it marks the fence with 에
울타리 as object takes 를 after a vowel
examples: 저 집은 울타리가 낮아요.
That house has a low fence.
simple description with 가
강아지가 울타리 안에서만 뛰어놀아요.
The puppy plays only inside the fence.
everyday: 울타리 안 (inside the fence) + 만 (only)
옆집과 우리 집 사이에 울타리를 쳐서 경계를 나눴어요.
We put up a fence between next door and us to divide the boundary.
real situation: 울타리를 치다 (put up a fence) + 경계를 나누다
nuance: 울타리 is a light, often see-through *fence/hedge* — wooden slats, wire, or a row of shrubs — that gently marks where a yard or field ends. It is native Korean (no hanja). Its core collocation is 울타리를 치다 ('put up a fence'), and figuratively it means a protective boundary ('가족이라는 울타리' = the shelter of family). Distinguish it sharply by *solidity and material*: a 울타리 is open and low, whereas 담 / 담장 is a *solid masonry wall* (brick or concrete) enclosing a property — English 'fence/wall' blurs these, but a thing you can see through is 울타리, a thing you cannot is 담. Don't confuse it with 벽 either: 벽 is a *building's* wall (a room side or partition), while 울타리 stands outdoors around open ground. Register is neutral, slightly rural/homely. The particle pitfall: leaning against or blooming on the fence uses 에 (울타리에 기대요), and because the word ends in a vowel its subject marker is 가, never 이.

mistakes: Using 이 after the vowel: 울타리이 낮아요. After a vowel use 가 (울타리가 낮아요).
Confusing 울타리 with 담. 담/담장 is a solid masonry boundary wall; 울타리 is a light open fence or hedge. Choose by whether you can see through it.
Using 울타리 for a room's wall. The wall of a building/room is 벽; 울타리 is an outdoor boundary around a yard.

usage: There is a lock on the front gate.
the lock is on the gate → 에
I wait at the front gate.
대문 as object takes 을; 잠그다 (lock)
examples: 우리 집 대문은 파란색이에요.
Our front gate is blue.
simple description with 이다
할머니가 대문 앞에서 저를 기다리고 계셨어요.
Grandma was waiting for me in front of the gate.
everyday: 대문 앞 + honorific progressive 기다리고 계시다
밤늦게 들어올 때는 대문을 꼭 잠그고 들어와요.
When you come in late at night, be sure to lock the gate behind you.
real situation: 잠그고 들어오다 (lock then come in), instruction register
nuance: 대문 is the main *outer gate* of a house — the large door in the boundary wall through which you pass from the street into the 마당. It is Sino-Korean 大門, literally 大 'big' + 門 'gate/door' = 'big gate', which fits its sense as the principal entrance to the property. The crucial contrast is 대문 vs 현관: 대문 is *outside* on the property line (street → yard), while 현관 is the *building's* own entry hall where you take your shoes off (yard → inside); a detached house has both, but an apartment has only a 현관 and no 대문. Also distinguish the generic 문 ('door/gate' of anything) — 대문 specifically names the big front gate. 대문 collocates with 열다/닫다 (open/close), 잠그다 (lock), 두드리다 (knock), and 대문 앞 (in front of the gate). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't call the apartment building's entry door a 대문 (that's the 현관/공동현관), and keep 에 for what sits on the gate (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions like waiting (대문에서 기다려요).

Saying 대문에서 자물쇠가 있어요. A lock's presence takes 에 (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action such as 기다리다.
